title: A convert in New York (1938)
hookLine: he reads philosophy, walks into a church, and is baptized

lines: A BOOK HE NEARLY THREW OUT.
I WANT TO BECOME A CATHOLIC.
cards: New York, 1937. Merton is at Columbia, and he buys a book for a class: a history of medieval philosophy. On the train home he opens it and sees the little Latin stamp saying a Catholic censor approved it.
He's so annoyed he nearly throws it out the window. He doesn't. He reads it, and one idea in it cracks something open.
A year later he's standing in a priest's doorway on a rainy afternoon, saying: I want to become a Catholic.

teach.b: First, the idea. The book was Étienne Gilson's The Spirit of Medieval Philosophy. Merton had assumed God was a vague, fuzzy feeling.

Gilson showed him the medieval idea that God is not one more thing in the universe, but being itself, the reason anything exists at all. Merton later wrote that this gave him a whole new respect for the faith.
Second, the friends: a professor named Mark Van Doren, a poet friend named Robert Lax.

teach.h: A TEACHER, A POET, A HINDU MONK.
teach.b: And a surprise: a Hindu monk visiting New York, called Bramachari, who told him to read Augustine's Confessions and The Imitation of Christ, the great books of his own Western tradition. Third, the church.
One Sunday in August 1938 he went, alone, to Mass at Corpus Christi Church near the university. He left before the end, nervous, and walked down the street happier than he'd felt in years.

Weeks later, reading about the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins becoming a Catholic, he put the book down, walked through the rain to the rectory, and asked. On November 16, 1938, he was baptized. Fourth, the word.
Convert comes from the Latin convertere, to turn around. The Catholic twist: the turning isn't only the person's own work.
In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him." Looking back, Merton saw it the same way. A book, a teacher, a monk, a Mass.
Someone was drawing him the whole time.

how: Adults who become Catholic today usually walk a path of study and prayer called the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, and are often baptized or received into the Church at the Easter Vigil.

games.q: you're Merton, reading about a poet's conversion on a rainy afternoon. something in you says, now. what do you do?
o: walk through the rain to the priest's house and ask
games.why: he put the book down, walked to the rectory, and said he wanted to become a Catholic. he was baptized that November.

practice: Go back to the first time faith, or the question of God, caught your attention: a person, a place, a song, a funeral, a book you almost threw away.
It doesn't matter if you're sure of anything now; find that first thread, look at it for a moment, and ask whose hand was in it. If you pray, you can say thank you for it.

wordCard.voice: Convert. From the Latin convertere, to turn around. For Merton, a turning that took years, through a book, some friends, and one quiet Mass. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: to turn around, the root of convert and conversion.

carryVoice: Your line: someone was drawing him. The week's lines: clothed in beauty, first smoke then flame, judged on love, arise and come, the night is a way, restless is a start. That's the week.
